subject: Pathology
summary: Essential thrombocythaemia (ET) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm causing sustained high platelet counts. It carries risk of thrombosis and bleeding despite the platelet excess.

sections.p: ET is defined by a persistent platelet count >450 ×10⁹/L, bone‑marrow showing megakaryocytic proliferation, and exclusion of secondary causes.
b: WHO criteria: high platelets, megakaryocyte morphology, JAK2/CALR/MPL mutation, no other myeloproliferative disease.

t.b: Is the platelet count >450 ×10⁹/L? Confirms thrombocytosis; very high counts (>1 000 ×10⁹/L) suggest ET.
Is a clonal mutation present? Positive result supports primary ET; negative does not exclude it.
Does marrow show enlarged, mature megakaryocytes with clustering? Confirms ET; if unavailable, rely on peripheral criteria and mutation status.

sections.p: Risk stratification guides therapy: low, intermediate‑1, intermediate‑2, and high risk based on age, prior thrombosis, and platelet count.
b: Low risk: age <60, no thrombosis, platelets <1 000 ×10⁹/L.
High risk: age ≥60 or prior thrombosis or platelets >1 000 ×10⁹/L.

sections.p: ET is clonal; most cases have a driver mutation. Secondary thrombocytosis must be excluded first.
b: Reactive causes: infection, iron deficiency, post‑splenectomy, inflammation, HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or have microvascular symptoms, thrombosis, or paradoxical bleeding.
Lab and imaging confirm diagnosis, assess risk, and look for complications.

t.b: Is thrombocytosis isolated? Helps rule out leukocytosis or anemia suggesting other MPDs.
Is iron deficiency present? Low ferritin can cause reactive thrombocytosis; treat before labeling ET.
Is there evidence of thrombosis? Guides urgent anticoagulation.

sections.p: Complications arise from clot formation or bleeding due to dysfunctional platelets.
Treat the clone, reduce platelet count, and prevent thrombosis while avoiding excess bleeding.
b: Low‑risk: low‑dose aspirin only if no bleeding risk.
Intermediate/high‑risk: cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea preferred; interferon if young or pregnant).
Avoid anagrelide as first line due to cardiovascular side‑effects.

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression to myelofibrosis or acute leukemia and adjusts therapy.
b: CBC every 3–6 months; repeat mutation testing if disease evolves.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and influenza; counsel on smoking cessation.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause high platelets or similar symptoms.
Laboratory and clinical findings may be deceptive.
b: Very high platelets can paradoxically cause bleeding due to platelet dysfunction.
JAK2‑negative ET may be missed if mutation testing is not performed.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, or limb pain suggesting arterial thrombosis.
Severe headache or visual loss indicating cerebral ischemia.
Unexplained bruising or bleeding with extremely high platelet count.

faq.q: Why can ET cause bleeding despite high platelets?
faq.a: Platelets become dysfunctional at very high counts, impairing clot formation.

faq.q: Is aspirin safe in all ET patients?
faq.a: Only if they have no high‑risk bleeding features; aspirin can worsen hemorrhage when platelets >1 500 ×10⁹/L.

faq.q: When is interferon preferred over hydroxyurea?
faq.a: In young patients, women planning pregnancy, or when hydroxyurea is contraindicated.

exam: List the WHO diagnostic criteria for essential thrombocythaemia.
Explain how you would risk‑stratify a newly diagnosed ET patient.
Describe the first‑line cytoreductive therapy for high‑risk ET and why alternatives are avoided.
